messages.subject: Multistate analysis
messages.body_plain:
I hope this email finds you well. I am a graduate student at Missouri State University, currently conducting research on the survival and detection probability of the Egyptian Tortoise, a critically endangered species in the Mediterranean basin. I have meticulously gathered data from five different sites over the past two decades.

I am writing to request an assistance in performing a multistate analysis, particularly in transitioning from less than one year to juvenile, and from juvenile to male or female states.

I am currently based in Egypt, where I serve as an ecologist in the Zaranik protected area. I have the necessary codes and JAGS models, but I have encountered some errors in running the R code. I have also not yet developed the R code for the new transition from less than one year to juvenile and from Juvenile to male or female. Your assistance would be invaluable, as my advisor needs this analysis and I have been stuck on this step for over a month developing the R code.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Sincerely,

Basem Motwaly

messages.body_plain: I have been working to fit a Jolly-Seber model to individual-level capture histories in a state-space formulation following chapter 10 of the BPA book (K&S 2012).  My target of interest is abundance estimation, so I have been employing data augmentation throughout this process.  I am now interested in fitting the model for a large capture-history data set (dimensions: ~7000 rows, 500 cols).  I have some flexibility in analysis, as I am not interested in individual-level effects.  Because of this, I would like to translate the state-space likelihood of the Jolly-Seber to the m-array formulation, but I have had considerable trouble working through this conversion.  I am aware of the likelihood's generalized expression in chapter 18 of "the brown book" (WNC 2002), but have still struggled with translating this for use in JAGS in a format robust to work through my dataset.  Is anyone aware of where the m-array likelihood of any Jolly-Seber parameterization has been worked out in BUGS?

messages.body_plain:
Quantitative Research Ecologist Contractor

The USGS Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center is seeking a quantitative ecologist to co-develop a study design to understand how various habitat treatments influence pollinator communities. The ecologist will be expected to 1) use hierarchical modeling techniques to assess power of various study designs, 2) simulate and analyze data (e.g., occupancy models or community occupancy models), 3) manipulate large, spatial datasets, 4) prepare manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals, 5) communicate with partners to identify and integrate multiple objectives into an optimal study design. There are also opportunities for collaboration on related pollinator and ungulate projects. Ideal candidate has a strong background in applied math and statistics as well as a demonstrated record of applying quantitative approaches to applied questions in ecology.

 Position is open to current graduate students or recent graduates eligible to work as a student contractor (MS or PhD preferred). Graduates that completed their degree within the past year are eligible to work as student contractors. Contracts can cover up to 1 (PhD) or 2 (MS) years of work. The start date, hours (30-40) and work location are negotiable (remote or West Glacier, MT); applicants that can start in 2023 are preferred. We seek to create a diverse team.

 If interested, please send your resume, cover letter, and contact information for 3 or more references to Tabitha Graves, tgraves @ usgs.gov <http://usgs.gov>. Please include your dates of availability and graduation date in the cover letter. Applications will be accepted until the position is filled.

Wages range from ~$24.08-$35.64/hr depending on experience and federal rate.

Requirements:

·        Analyses of hierarchical models (e.g., occupancy, abundance models accounting for detection)

·        Strong quantitative analytical skills

·        Strong scientific writing skills

·        U.S. citizen

Desirable qualifications:

·        Proficiency in R, JAGS, NIMBLE or similar

·        Expertise in hierarchical models, Bayesian approaches, advanced statistics

·        Expertise in relational databases, large data management

·        Expertise in community and population ecology

·        Expertise in pollination ecology and vegetation

·        Expertise in disturbance ecology, restoration, fire, weed treatments, or grazing

·        Expertise in prairie and sagebrush systems

·        Record of publication in peer-reviewed journals

·        MS or PhD in ecology, wildlife science, statistics, or related degree

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I have data from a spatial capture resight study based on the iterative re-sighting study by Ritterson et al. 2021 <https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/pubs/jrnl/2021/nrs_2021_ritterson_002.pdf> and I have successfully estimated apparent survival like in the study. I now want to explore the possibility of obtaining density for the species within each study site and I thought about implementing the spatial mark-resight framework found in Kane et al. 2015 <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10531-015-1012-7> which is based on Chapters 18-19 by Royle et al.'s book <https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780124059399/spatial-capture-recapture>.

My question for this group is, based on this method where the trap locations are not fixed or constant across a study period (see image below with each point representing a resight point count and each color the occasion), would this data be inadequate for this framework?

I thought about assigning a point by compiling all the points that fall within a 50 m hexagon (as the protocol of resighting iteratively makes you move ~50 m in search for your marked individuals) but this means that some cells will have more info than others.

Any comments welcome
Fabi

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am currently working on an age-specific multi-state model with multinomial likelihood. The dataset comprises information from >3500 marked vultures of various ages, incorporating recaptures and observations both within and outside our study site, along with dead recoveries spanning 29 occasions. The primary objective is to estimate the site-specific survival rates for two age classes: non-adults (0 to 4 years) and adults (>4 years). The states are encoded as follows: alive as a non-adult at site A (1), alive as an adult at site A (2), alive as a non-adult at site B (3), alive as an adult at site B (4), and recovered dead (5).

Here is the code and .csv:

library(jagsUI) library(IPMbook)

MS <- read.table("CAT_5states.csv", header=T, sep=",")

marr <- marray(MS, unobs = 1)

# Bundle data
# There are 5 states in MS but we added an non-observable state "6"
# to calculate the absorbing state or long-dead state.
mns <- 6
jags.data <- list(marr=marr, n.occasions=ncol(MS), relm=rowSums(marr), mns=mns, zerom=matrix(0, mns, mns),
                  onesm=diag(mns), recap = c(rep(1,3),2:29)) # first two occasions there were no recaptures

sink("marray.jags")

model {

# Priors and linear models

    logit(s1.cat <http://s1.cat>[t]) <- suv1.cat <http://suv1.cat> + epsilon1.cat <http://epsilon1.cat>[t]
      epsilon1.cat <http://epsilon1.cat>[t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.s)
    logit(s2.cat <http://s2.cat>[t]) <- suv2.cat <http://suv2.cat> + epsilon2.cat <http://epsilon2.cat>[t]

Hi Diego,

here are some observations about your model:
Since you are using the multinomial likelihood, there is no need to include the recovery process in the state transitions. Therefore, you should remove r[t] from the transitions to state 5, and the transitions from states 1..4 to state 6 must all be 0.
The recovery shall be modeled here: pom[5,t] <- r[t]
Individuals that are long-time dead (state 6), need to stay there, so the transition from state 6 to 6 must be 1

I have not run the model with these adaptations, so please try and see whether the model runs. If it does still not run, there may be additional issues….

Kind regards

Michael

Dear Friends and Colleagues (and apologies for cross-posting),

We are very pleased to announce that we are taking applications for the fifth intake of our new MSc in Statistical Ecology detailed in the attached leaflet.

The MSc aims to give students:
a sound understanding of the statistical foundations of modern methods in statistical ecology
the knowledge and skills to use these methods effectively
experience of applying them to real-world problems, under the supervision of experts, some of whom are leading researchers in this field

The Programme involves two semesters of taught courses and a 3-month summer research dissertation. It is taught by staff at the interdisciplinary Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/). The summer dissertation includes optional placements with collaborators in the UK or abroad, to give students experience of dealing with real-world problems in statistical ecology.

More information is available here: https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/subjects/statistics/statistical-ecology-msc/

For any additional information, please direct enquiries to ma...@st-andrews.ac.uk or to me, the program coordinator, cs...@st-andrews.ac.uk

Chris
